doc.title: Henry Johnson interviewed by Michael Woods, Majesty of the Seas, May 30, 1995

title: Music as community and universal language
summary: Woods and Johnson discuss music creating community in audiences, a Creator working through musicians, and music as conversation between player and listener.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: And now here’s something else that I would like you to talk about. You talked about your Gospel experience. You talked about your rhythm & blues experience. You talked about the blues making a person not feel alone. And then when I think of jazz I think of probably the most sophisticated improvisatory music in the world that’s been lifted to the level of an art form. But to me, it still develops this communal effect. Like when I go to a black Gospel church. And sometimes even if it’s a preacher that I don’t like, if the soprano is singing real good, why I’ve already got my message. You know what I mean? And that can give me a sense of community. And make me feel a part of a whole. Just one sometimes can do that for me. And have you played your guitar and seen that happen in an audience? Just without your conversing with them. They don’t know anything about you, they just hear you play your guitar and that gives that sense of community.

Yeah. I see it happen all the time in most places that I play. And I don’t know if I’m doing it or — I think that the Creator of us all is using musicians as a tool to let that goodness flow through. You know and if we take our egos out of the way, it just comes through and hits you and creates something for you. You know you identify with it. For me I know that I’ve been in certain situations where I was playing on stage and people were sitting up front. And I know that this guy probably was, him and his lady were fighting before they got there. Because he probably didn’t want to pay the cover charge or something like that you know? But the moment that we hit one of those songs he starts, a smile on his face, starts tapping his feet [inaudible] And when they left there they

were smiling and he was really happy that he came, because the music made him feel good, along with her. So it changes people. It’s a universal language that no matter what country we go in, whether they speak the language or not, the music is the language that everybody speaks.

You know speaking of language, I’ll share this with you and then I want you to give me one of your examples. Sometimes you know I will go to hear a great musician. And I won’t know the person personally. But they’ll be up there playing and of course I’m a musician so I’ll say to myself, okay now I need him to go on up in the register right now. Soon as I think that he goes up there and starts burning. I said now he’s playing a million notes. Not I need him to back off on that technique and just give me a blues lick. And just about that time he’ll cut off them power techniques and play something funky and bluesy. And I go now this guy’s reading my mind, you know? He’s giving me just what I want when I want it. And then, you know he’ll finish the song or maybe if I listen to a set then I’ll say I almost feel like I’ve had a conversation with that person. You know because the music is language.

Yeah it is. I think so too. It’s because you’re a musician and you speak the same language. And you’re thinking the way they will be thinking because you are both tapped into that creative flow. See even when you don’t have your axe in your hand, you’re still playing, you know? Because your mind is the thing that plays. The instrument could be a block of wood or anything else, the instrument just goes in your hand to get out what’s in your mind. And so even when you’re watching somebody else, your mind is still playing. And you’re both tapped into the same thing. I do the same thing all the time. I sense that too you know. So I know exactly what you’re talking about.
